lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Trade: Brokerage, STT, GST, and Exchange Charges in India

markDefs.definition: The statement a broker issues after a trade settles, itemizing the trade price along with every charge applied to it.

children.text: Buy 100 shares of a stock and sell the same 100 shares a week later, and the two

your broker sends will not look alike. The buy side carries a charge the sell side does not. The sell side carries a tax rate that, for an intraday trade, would have been different on the buy side. Lesson 1 treated transaction costs as a single number to subtract from returns. This lesson opens that number up and walks through exactly what it is made of, in the order a real trade actually incurs it.
Following One Trade From Order to Contract Note

body.title: The Life of a Single Order

events.title: Order Placed
events.description: You submit a buy or sell order through your broker's terminal, for example Zerodha Kite, Upstox Pro, or a broker API.

events.title: Order Matched
events.description: The exchange (NSE or BSE) matches your order against a counterparty in the order book at the traded price.

events.title: Charges Computed
events.description: Brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty, and GST are calculated on the executed value, not the price you originally quoted.

events.title: T+1 Settlement
events.description: Funds and securities move between accounts through the clearing corporation, currently on a T+1 cycle for Indian equities.

events.title: Contract Note Generated
events.description: The broker issues an itemized statement showing the trade price and every charge applied to it.

children.text: Step 3 is where a backtest either gets honest or stays fictional. Everything charged there needs to be reproduced in code before a backtest's numbers mean anything. Here is what actually gets computed.
The Six Line Items on Every Contract Note

body.text: STT, exchange transaction charges, stamp duty, and GST are all set by the government, the exchanges, or the GST Council, and every one of them has changed at least once in a past Union Budget or regulatory circular. The rates used in the worked example below reflect commonly cited recent levels. Before relying on a cost model for real trading or tax purposes, check the exact current rates on your broker's contract note or the relevant exchange circular.

children.text: Worked Example: A ₹1 Lakh Round Trip in a Nifty 50 Stock, Delivery

Buy ₹1,00,000 worth of a Nifty 50 stock as a delivery trade through a discount broker, then sell the same ₹1,00,000 worth later. Holding the price flat isolates the pure cost of trading, with no profit or loss mixed in.

children.text: Why the Buy Side and Sell Side Are Not Identical

Stamp duty is charged only when you buy, never when you sell, which is why the buy side above costs more even though the trade values are identical. STT runs the other way for intraday trades, where it is charged only on the sell leg and at a lower rate than delivery STT, because the government treats intraday activity differently from investment. A strategy's average holding period and whether it trades delivery or intraday therefore changes not just how much it pays in costs, but which line item dominates.

body.text: This asymmetry matters for backtest design specifically. A cost function that applies one flat rate to every trade, ignoring the buy/sell and delivery/intraday distinctions, will misprice a long-short strategy differently from a long-only one, since a long-short book generates far more sell-side (and short-entry) volume relative to a simple buy-and-hold book.

children.text: Delivery vs Intraday: Same Trade, Different Cost Structure

body.title: Two Trade Types, Two Cost Profiles

columns.label: Delivery (Investment)
points: STT charged on both buy and sell, at the higher delivery rate
Stamp duty charged on the buy side
Shares move into your demat account, no intraday square-off needed

columns.label: Intraday
points: STT charged only on the sell side, at a lower rate than delivery
Stamp duty still charged on the buy side, but at a lower intraday rate
Brokerage typically a flat fee per order, or a percentage, whichever is lower
Position must be squared off the same day, or it auto-converts to delivery

children.text: None of this is difficult to encode once the mechanics are clear, it is a handful of percentage rates applied to trade value, with a couple of if/else branches for buy vs sell and delivery vs intraday. Chapter 2 builds exactly that cost function, generalizes it across cash equity, futures, and options, and shows how to wire it directly into a backtest so every simulated trade pays what a real trade would have paid.

body.title: Quick Check
body.prompt: You buy ₹2,00,000 worth of a stock as a delivery trade. STT on a delivery buy is charged at 0.1% of trade value. How much STT, in rupees, do you pay on this buy order alone?
body.explanation: 0.1% of ₹2,00,000 is ₹200. Because this is a delivery trade, an identical STT charge of ₹200 will also apply when you eventually sell, unlike stamp duty, which would apply only on this buy side.

body.text: A single trade is not one charge, it is six: brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty, and GST, applied asymmetrically across the buy and sell side and across delivery and intraday. Get the anatomy right and an accurate cost model becomes mechanical; get it wrong and your backtest misprices every trade it simulates.

points: Every NSE or BSE trade carries six identifiable charges: brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI turnover fees, stamp duty, and GST, applied by different bodies on different sides of the trade.
Stamp duty applies only to the buy side; STT applies to both sides for delivery but only the sell side for intraday, so the buy and sell legs of an otherwise identical trade cost different amounts.
On a ₹1,00,000 delivery round trip through a discount broker, STT alone accounted for roughly ₹200 of the ~₹222 total cost, making it the single largest line item even with zero brokerage.
These rates are set by the government, the exchanges, and the GST Council, and have changed before, so a cost model belongs in a config you can update, not hardcoded once and forgotten.
